statement: Towers of cubes stand on a grid of 2 rows and 3 columns. From left to right, the back row has towers of 1, 3 and 2 cubes, and the front row has towers of 2, 1 and 1 cubes. Looking from straight in front, you see a flat shape made of squares. How many squares does it have?

choices.misconception: I gave the height of the tallest tower instead of counting the squares in the view.
I counted only the front row and forgot that taller towers behind it show above it.
I added the tallest tower in each row, 3 and 2, instead of looking at each column.
I counted one square for each tower, which is the view from above, not from the front.

hints: Look at one column at a time, front and back together.
From the front, a back tower hides behind the front tower in its column unless it is taller. So each column shows as many squares as its taller tower. Do this for all three columns and add.
The columns show the taller of 1 and 2, the taller of 3 and 1, and the taller of 2 and 1: that is 2, 3 and 2 squares.

solutions.reliable: Each column of the front view is as tall as the taller tower in that column, because the shorter one is hidden behind it. Left column: the taller of 1 and 2 is 2. Middle column: the taller of 3 and 1 is 3. Right column: the taller of 2 and 1 is 2. The view has 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 squares. The transferable idea: a view from one side keeps only the tallest tower in each line of sight.

whyOnTest: Views questions check that you know what hides behind what: from the front, only the tallest tower in each column counts.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
